1365.dq: The tonal system of Mandinka, like that of the other Manding languages, is characterized by strong restrictions on the possible tone sequences within the limits of various types of units (roots, complex lexemes, words) and by a complex system of tone sandhi.

1366.prule: Left-aligned weight-sensitive iamb: primary stress on the second syllable of the word unless the first syllable is heavy (long vowel or coda glottal stop), in which case stress is initial; never on the third syllable or beyond; monosyllables stressed. Secondary stress: a further left-aligned iambic foot immediately to the right of the primary-stress foot.
1366.srule: One secondary stress on the iambic foot immediately after the primary-stress foot: on the second syllable after the primary-stressed syllable, unless the syllable right after the primary stress is heavy (long vowel or coda glottal stop), which then takes it (clash allowed: rúuhaare [(ˈⁿduː).(ˌhaː).ɾe]; mashkáshkapka [(mã.ˈʃka).(ʃka.ˌpka)]). evidence_works.detail: Two-page summary sheet with no stated data-collection method; its only sources are the three works in its bibliography (Trifkovič 1969, Gaved 2020, Kanfome 2016), and it cites Gaved (2020: 11) inline on vowels and Trifkovič (1969) on consonants and on the pre-accentual schwa. §4 Prosodie, p. 2: 'Le mankanya n'a pas de système tonal mais possède un accent de mot qui marque en règle générale la première syllabe de la base lexicale du mot (c'est-à-dire pratiquement la première ou la deuxième syllabe du mot, selon sa structure morphologique).' This is Gaved's root-initial rule (record quote §2.10: 'Normally the accent is placed on the first syllable of the root') restated in French, with the word-position consequence (first or second syllable of the word depending on prefixation) spelled out. §2 Voyelles, p. 2 adds 'une tendance à la réduction de [ə] en syllabe initiale non accentuée', matching Gaved's preaccentual schwa (record quote §2.2.3, p. 12). It also agrees with the no-tone class. It says nothing about secondary stress, so sec_status stays on Trifkovič 1969.

tn.quote: Le matal est une langue tonale. Je suppose que, du point de vue phonémique, le matal ait deux niveaux de tons: haut (H) et bas (B).36 En plus, sur le plan phonétique, on peut entendre le ton moyen (M) et des tons descendants ou montants. Le rendement fonctionnel des tons sur le plan lexicale est faible: il n’y a que quelques rares paires minimales, dont la plus fréquente est celle entre /ɡàj/ [ɡàj] (B) maison et /ɡáj/ [ɡâj] (H) bouche. C’est plutôt au niveau grammatical que les tons jouent un rôle distinctif … /dá/ [dá] (H) PASSE (‘éloigné’)37 et /dà/ [dà] FUTUR.
tn.translation: Matal is a tone language. I assume that, phonemically, Matal has two tone levels: high (H) and low (B). In addition, phonetically one can hear a mid tone (M) and falling or rising tones. The functional load of tones at the lexical level is low: there are only a few rare minimal pairs, the most frequent being /ɡàj/ [ɡàj] (L) 'house' vs /ɡáj/ [ɡâj] (H) 'mouth'. It is rather at the grammatical level that tones play a distinctive role … /dá/ [dá] (H) PAST ('remote') and /dà/ [dà] FUTURE.

tn.quote: All such words have a single stress on either the first or second syllable; there is no secondary stress. I assume, however, that the mora is actually the stress-bearing unit ... 1385.tone: Phonemic two-level tone (H vs L); M is a positional variant of L (L raised to M before a following nonhigh tone). Tone distinguishes perfective/imperfective verb stems (fó/fò 'go'). 1387.dq: Word-level stress differences are not particularly pronounced in Mangap-Mbula. To the ear, many sequences of syllables seem almost evenly stressed. Slight differences in amplitude can, however, be heard. The placement of stress is predictable, but several interacting rules are required.
1387.dloc: Ch. 2 Phonology, sec. 2.6 'Stress placement', pp. 76-80; vowel length analysis sec. 2.2.2.2 pp. 31-33
1387.heavy: a following 'vocoid cluster or lengthened vocoid' (Rule 40), i.e. a syllable with a heterorganic vowel cluster/diphthong or a long vowel; surface length is contrastive ([moto] '2SG fear' vs [mo:to] 'snake', [molo] 'long' vs [mo:lo] 'ant sp.'), though Bugenhagen derives it by Penultimate Lengthening of an underlying single vowel (/moto/ -> [mo:to]) with the short counterpart epenthetic (/mto/ -> [moto]), so long vowels occur only morpheme-penultimately; closed syllables ([tomtom], [posop]) do not attract stress
1387.dflt: initial syllable (extrametrical verbal subject prefix ignored, Rule 39) in words of up to three syllables; in words of four or more syllables the head of the penultimate binary trochaic foot, feet parsed left-to-right (Rules 42-43): 4-syll initial (nákabasi 'axe'), 6-syll third syllable (weŋgarŋgá:raŋana 'yellow'); for odd-parity long words the prose ('In words of three or more syllables which contain an odd number of syllables, the last Foot is defective... Such defective Feet are not stressed. Among Feet, the penultimate Foot receives the greatest stress') implies third syllable in 5-syll and fifth in 7-syll words (and correctly yields initial in 3-syll words), but no monomorphemic 5- or 7-syllable example is given
1387.prule: Default word-initial primary stress (Rule 39), with verbal Subject prefixes extrametrical (overridden for two-phoneme prefixes before a monosyllabic stem, Rule 41); stress shifts off the initial onto a following syllable containing a vocoid cluster (diphthong) or lengthened vocoid (Rule 40, e.g. [tomo:to] 'man' stressed on the long second syllable vs [mutu] 'island' initial); in words of four or more syllables binary trochaic feet are built left-to-right, foot heads get secondary stress and the head of the penultimate foot gets primary stress (Rules 42-43, e.g. nakabasi 'axe' initial, weŋgarŋga:raŋana 'yellow' third syllable).
1387.srule: In words of four or more syllables, two-syllable trochaic feet are built left to right from the first syllable (extrametrical Subject prefixes ignored); the first syllable of every foot carries secondary stress, the head of the penultimate foot being promoted to primary, and a single-syllable final foot in odd-parity words is unstressed (Rules 42-43: [nákabàsi] 'axe', [wèŋgarŋgá:raŋàna] 'yellow'). An internal word boundary before nominaliser -ŋa, before the accusative enclitics =i/=u, and inside complete reduplications adds a secondary stress on the following element (pá:za#ŋà-na, ti#ré#ì, ti-kís#kìs).

dqtr.text: In Guarani the default is the oxytone word (the stressed syllable is the last), so the accent is written only on proparoxytones or paroxytones.... The tone group corresponds to the grammatical phrase (as in French), not to the word itself... So the general stress pattern is the following: within the phrase, the last syllable that accepts stress is nuclear.

1388.dq: Em guarani, o padrão é a palavra oxítona (a sílaba tônica é a última), portanto o acento é só escrito nas proparoxítonas ou paroxítonas. ... O grupo tonal corresponde ao sintagma gramatical (como no francês), não à palavra em si ... Portanto, o padrão geral da tonicidade é o seguinte: dentro do sintagma, a última sílaba que aceita o acento é nuclear.
1388.prule: Default pattern is oxytone: the stressed syllable is the last syllable of the word ('o padrão é a palavra oxítona'); but the stress group is the syntactic phrase, not the word: within the phrase the last syllable that can accept stress is nuclear; atonic words (certain postpositions, tense/aspect/modal particles) never bear stress, so if the phrase ends in one the nucleus falls earlier. Lexically paroxytone/proparoxytone words (some native, e.g. ára 'day', kóropi 'this way', kuery 'collective'; several Portuguese loans) keep non-final stress and are written with an acute accent.
1388.srule: Within the tone group (= syntactic phrase; hedged 'comumente/geralmente/tende a') secondary stresses, weaker than the nucleus, alternate with unstressed syllables leftward from the nuclear (final stressable) syllable, forming iambic feet; none on the phrase-initial syllable, so phrases begin with one or two unstressed syllables (ex. kova'e oo porã py: secondary on syllables 3 and 5, primary on 7, enclitic py atonic).

1389.prule: Penultimate stress, as in Quichua; stress shifts rightward as suffixes are added so that it stays on the penult of the full word (vaca [ˈbaka]... vacagucunamantami [bakaɡukunamanˈtami]). Phonetically realized as an L+H* pitch accent on/around the penult at the prosodic-word level (Stewart 2015). No weight condition stated.

In reduplicated pairs the first member carries a secondary accent, the second the primary.

1390.prule: Dynamic (stress) accent, in place since the Hellenistic/Roman period, continuing the lexically and morphologically determined positions of the Ancient Greek accent; position not predictable from syllable count or weight, but limited to one of the last three syllables of the word ('standard rule'); medieval changes move stress by synizesis ([-'ia] > [-'ja]) and by paradigm levelling ('columnar stress').

1391.prule: No phonological placement rule is stated in either primary. Both grammars treat paroxytone (penultimate) stress as the unmarked default of their transcription and mark the accent individually on oxytones (words ending in a stressed vowel; word-final ǫ < stressed ă/â is always stressed) and on proparoxytones: a Romance/Romanian-type lexically specified stress within the last three syllables, penult most frequent, mobile in verb paradigms (Capidan passim: forms 'cu accentul pe tulpină' vs 'cu accentul pe terminațiune').
1391.quote: Capidan 1925 p. 96: "Accentul s'a însemnat numai la cuvintele terminate într'o vocală accentuată, afară de cuvintele sfârșite în ǫ care rezultă totdeauna dintr'un sunet accentuat, și la proparoxitoane." ... Papahagi 1902 (Glosar): "Tote cuvintele neaccentuate, atât în glosar cât şi în texte, se cetesc cu accentul pe penultima."
1391.loc: Capidan 1925 'Dialectul meglenoromân' (second part), A. Fonologia, Sunetele, transcription conventions, p. 96 (Commons p. 95); Papahagi 1902, Glosar, introductory note (archive.org)

1391.exq_: No rule is stated; the penultimate reading is an orthographic default, with oxytones and proparoxytones (open classes) marked word by word: "Accentul s'a însemnat numai la cuvintele terminate într'o vocală accentuată ... și la proparoxitoane."
